solution:
The statement is correct.

Pressure-volume work is given by \(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V\). Expansion into a vacuum is a free expansion, that is, expansion against zero opposing force, so \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Hence \(W = -0 \times \Delta V = 0\), however large the volume change may be.

The volume of the gas does increase, but a volume change by itself does no work: work is done only when the system is linked to the surroundings by an external pressure that has to be overcome. With nothing opposing the expansion, no energy is transferred as work.

The first law of thermodynamics is simply the law of conservation of energy: the total energy of a system and its surroundings remains constant when the system changes from an initial state to a final state. It is stated in several equivalent ways — energy of the universe remains constant; the total internal energy of an isolated system is constant; energy is neither created nor destroyed and can only be converted from one form into another.

Mathematically, if \(Q\) is the heat supplied to the system and \(W\) the work done on the system,
\(\Delta U = Q + W\)
where \(\Delta U\) is the increase in internal energy of the system.

The enthalpy of fusion \((\Delta_{fus}H)\) is the enthalpy change that occurs when one mole of a solid is converted into liquid without change in temperature at constant pressure.

For example,
\(\mathrm{H_2O(s) \longrightarrow H_2O(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta_{fus}H = +6.01\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) at \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

That is, 6.01 kJ of heat is absorbed when one mole of ice melts at \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 1 atm pressure. Fusion is endothermic, so \(\Delta_{fus}H\) is positive; the reverse process, freezing, releases the same quantity of heat.

The standard state of a substance is the form in which the substance is most stable at a pressure of 1 bar and at temperature 298 K. If the reaction involves species in solution, the standard state refers to 1 M concentration.

For example, the standard states of some elements and compounds are \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\), \(\mathrm{Hg(\mathit{l})}\), \(\mathrm{Na(s)}\) or \(\mathrm{C(graphite)}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH(\mathit{l})}\), \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2(g)}\), each at 1 bar and \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

The standard state is a reference condition, fixed so that the enthalpy changes of different reactions can be compared under a similar set of conditions.

For \(\mathrm{2H(g) \longrightarrow H_2(g)}\), \(\Delta S\) is NEGATIVE.

Two moles of free gaseous hydrogen atoms combine to give one mole of hydrogen molecules. The number of independent gaseous particles therefore falls from 2 to 1, and the atoms, which previously moved freely and independently, become bound together in pairs. Both changes reduce the disorder of the system, and entropy is the measure of that disorder, so \(\Delta S < 0\).

This is simply the reverse of the dissociation \(\mathrm{H_2(g) \longrightarrow 2H(g)}\), for which the chapter notes that larger disorder is associated with the separated H atoms than with the \(\mathrm{H_2}\) molecule, so that \(\Delta S\) is positive. Reversing a process reverses the sign of its entropy change.

The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of a system and its surroundings increases in a spontaneous process.

For the process to be spontaneous,
\(\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} > 0\)

It follows that \(\Delta S_{total} < 0\) for a nonspontaneous process and \(\Delta S_{total} = 0\) for a process at equilibrium.

If \(\Delta H\) is the enthalpy change accompanying a reaction in the system, then the enthalpy change of the surroundings is \(-\Delta H\), because the heat lost by the system is gained by the surroundings and vice versa.

The entropy change of the surroundings at temperature \(T\) is therefore
\(\Delta S_{surr} = -\dfrac{\Delta H}{T}\)

So an exothermic reaction \((\Delta H < 0)\) gives a positive \(\Delta S_{surr}\), and an endothermic reaction gives a negative \(\Delta S_{surr}\).

Such reactions are nonspontaneous at ALL temperatures.

From \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), if \(\Delta H\) is positive then the first term is positive, and if \(\Delta S\) is negative then \(-T\Delta S\) is also positive for every positive temperature.

\(\Delta G\) is therefore the sum of two positive quantities and is positive regardless of temperature. Since spontaneity requires \(\Delta G < 0\), no temperature can make such a reaction spontaneous.

The Gibbs energy change of a reaction at any composition is
\(\Delta G = \Delta G^0 + RT \ln Q\)
where \(Q\) is the reaction quotient and \(\Delta G^0\) is the standard Gibbs energy change.

When the reaction reaches equilibrium, \(\Delta G = 0\) and \(Q\) becomes the equilibrium constant \((K_c\) or \(K_p)\). Substituting,
\(0 = \Delta G^0 + RT \ln K_c\) and \(0 = \Delta G^0 + RT \ln K_p\)

Therefore
\(\Delta G^0 = -RT \ln K_c\) and \(\Delta G^0 = -RT \ln K_p\)

or, converting to common logarithms,
\(\Delta G^0 = -2.303\,RT \log_{10} K_c\) and \(\Delta G^0 = -2.303\,RT \log_{10} K_p\)

A large equilibrium constant thus corresponds to a large negative \(\Delta G^0\).

Entropy, denoted by \(S\), is a measure of molecular disorder or randomness of a system. The greater the disorder of a system, the larger is its entropy.

Quantitatively, the entropy change of a system is the amount of heat transferred to it in a reversible manner divided by the temperature in kelvin at which the transfer takes place:
\(\Delta S = \dfrac{Q_{rev}}{T}\)

Entropy is a state function — it depends only on the initial and final states of the system and not on the path connecting them.

Units : \(\mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\) (and \(\mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\) when quoted per mole).

In a chemical reaction bonds are broken in the reactants and new bonds are formed in the products. Breaking a bond absorbs energy and forming a bond releases it, so the reaction enthalpy is the difference between the two:

\(\Delta_r H^0 = \sum \Delta H^0(\text{reactant bonds}) - \sum \Delta H^0(\text{product bonds})\)

that is, the sum of the bond enthalpies of all bonds BROKEN minus the sum of the bond enthalpies of all bonds FORMED, each multiplied by the number of such bonds.

For example, for \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,HI(g)}\),
\(\Delta_r H^0 = [\Delta H^0(\mathrm{H\text{-}H}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{I\text{-}I})] - [2\Delta H^0(\mathrm{H\text{-}I})]\)

The calculation assumes all bonds of a given type are identical. It gives accurate results when reactants and products are diatomic molecules, for which the bond enthalpies are known accurately. For reactions involving polyatomic molecules the AVERAGE bond enthalpy has to be used (for example the average C-H bond enthalpy in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) is \(1665/4 = 416\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)), so the reaction enthalpy obtained this way is only approximate.

The standard enthalpy of combustion \((\Delta_c H^0)\) of a substance is the standard enthalpy change accompanying a reaction in which one mole of the substance in its standard state is completely oxidised.

Example :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_2(g) + \tfrac{5}{2}\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,CO_2(g) + H_2O(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -1300\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Here one mole of \(\mathrm{C_2H_2}\) is completely oxidised, so \(-1300\ \mathrm{kJ}\) is the standard enthalpy of combustion of \(\mathrm{C_2H_2(g)}\). Combustion is always exothermic, so \(\Delta_c H^0\) is negative.

The enthalpy of atomization \((\Delta_{atom}H)\) is the enthalpy change accompanying the dissociation of one mole of a gaseous substance into its atoms.

Examples :
\(\mathrm{Cl_2(g) \longrightarrow Cl(g) + Cl(g)}\); \(\Delta_{atom}H = 242\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(\mathrm{CH_4(g) \longrightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\); \(\Delta_{atom}H = 1660\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

For a diatomic molecule the enthalpy of atomization is the same as the bond enthalpy, since only one bond is broken.

The work done by a system at constant temperature and pressure is
\(W = -P\,\Delta V\)   (taking \(P_{ext} = P\))
\(= -P\,(V_2 - V_1) = -PV_2 + PV_1\)

If the gases behave ideally, then for \(n_1\) moles of gaseous reactants and \(n_2\) moles of gaseous products,
\(PV_1 = n_1RT\) and \(PV_2 = n_2RT\)

At constant temperature and pressure, substituting these gives
\(W = -n_2RT + n_1RT\)
\(= -(n_2 - n_1)\,RT\)
\(= -\Delta n_g RT\)

where \(\Delta n_g\) is the difference between the number of moles of gaseous products and gaseous reactants.

The sign of \(W\) follows from \(\Delta n_g\):
i. if \(n_2 > n_1\), \(\Delta n_g\) is positive and \(W < 0\), i.e. work is done BY the system;
ii. if \(n_1 > n_2\), \(\Delta n_g\) is negative and \(W > 0\), i.e. work is done ON the system;
iii. if \(n_1 = n_2\), \(\Delta n_g = 0\) and \(W = 0\), i.e. no \(PV\) work is done.

Consider a certain amount of gas at constant pressure \(P\) enclosed in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless, rigid movable piston of area \(A\), the gas occupying volume \(V_1\) at temperature \(T\).

On expansion the force exerted by the gas equals the area of the piston multiplied by the pressure with which the gas pushes against the piston. This pressure is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the external atmospheric pressure that opposes the movement, and has the value \(-P_{ext}\). Thus
\(f = -P_{ext} \times A\)   ...(1)

If the piston moves out a distance \(d\), the work done is force multiplied by distance,
\(W = f \times d\)   ...(2)

Substituting (1) into (2),
\(W = -P_{ext} \times A \times d\)   ...(3)

The product of the area of the piston and the distance it moves is the volume change of the system,
\(\Delta V = A \times d\)   ...(4)

Combining (3) and (4),
\(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V = -P_{ext}\,(V_2 - V_1)\)

When the gas expands, \(V_2 > V_1\) and \(W\) is negative — work is done by the system on the surroundings. When the gas is compressed, \(V_2 < V_1\) and \(W\) is positive — work is done on the system by the surroundings.

An intensive property is a property which is independent of the amount of matter present in a system.

Examples : pressure, temperature, surface tension, viscosity, melting point, boiling point, specific heat.

Density is intensive because it is the RATIO of two extensive properties:
\(\text{density} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\)

Mass and volume both depend on the amount of matter, and they change in the same proportion. If the amount of a substance is doubled, its mass doubles and its volume also doubles, so the ratio is unchanged. A drop of water and a bucket of the same water at the same temperature therefore have the same density, which is why density does not depend on how much matter is present and is an intensive property.

\(\mathrm{4\,CO(g) + 2\,NO_2(g) \longrightarrow 4\,CO_2(g) + N_2(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -1200\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The thermochemical equation shows that 1200 kJ of heat is evolved when 4 moles of CO react.

Molar mass of CO \(= 12 + 16 = 28\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(n = \dfrac{12\ \mathrm{g}}{28\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.4286\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Heat evolved \(= \dfrac{0.4286\ \mathrm{mol}}{4\ \mathrm{mol}} \times 1200\ \mathrm{kJ} = 128.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Hence about 128.6 kJ of heat is evolved (\(\Delta H = -128.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\), the negative sign showing the reaction is exothermic).

Consider \(n\) moles of an ideal gas enclosed in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless movable rigid piston. It expands isothermally and reversibly from initial volume \(V_1\) to final volume \(V_2\) at temperature \(T\).

During each step the external pressure \(P_{ext}\) is made infinitesimally smaller than the pressure \(P\) of the gas, by gradual removal of masses from the piston, so the volume increases by an infinitesimal amount \(dV\) in each single step. The work done in such a step is
\(dW = -P_{ext}\,dV\)   ...(1)

As the expansion is reversible, \(P\) is greater than \(P_{ext}\) by a very small quantity \(dP\),
\(P - P_{ext} = dP\) or \(P_{ext} = P - dP\)   ...(2)

Combining (1) and (2),
\(dW = -(P - dP)\,dV = -P\,dV + dP\,dV\)

Neglecting the product \(dP\,dV\), which is very small,
\(dW = -P\,dV\)   ...(3)

The total work for the whole expansion is the sum of the infinitesimal contributions of all the steps, obtained by integrating (3) between the initial and final states. This is the MAXIMUM work, the expansion being reversible:
\(W_{max} = -\displaystyle\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV\)

Using the ideal gas law \(PV = nRT\), so that \(P = nRT/V\),
\(W_{max} = -\displaystyle\int_{V_1}^{V_2} nRT\,\dfrac{dV}{V} = -nRT \displaystyle\int_{V_1}^{V_2} \dfrac{dV}{V}\)   (because \(T\) is constant)
\(= -nRT\,(\ln V_2 - \ln V_1)\)
\(= -nRT \ln \dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\)
\(= -2.303\,nRT \log_{10} \dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\)

At constant temperature \(P_1V_1 = P_2V_2\), so \(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = \dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\), giving the alternative form
\(W_{max} = -2.303\,nRT \log_{10} \dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\)

Enthalpy is defined as \(H = U + PV\), so at constant pressure
\(\Delta H = \Delta U + P\,\Delta V\)
\(= \Delta U + P\,(V_2 - V_1)\)
\(= \Delta U + PV_2 - PV_1\)

where \(V_1\) is the volume of the gas-phase reactants and \(V_2\) that of the gaseous products.

Assuming the reactants and products behave ideally, and taking \(n_1\) moles of gaseous reactants and \(n_2\) moles of gaseous products, the ideal gas equation gives
\(PV_1 = n_1RT\) and \(PV_2 = n_2RT\)

Substituting these,
\(\Delta H = \Delta U + n_2RT - n_1RT\)
\(= \Delta U + (n_2 - n_1)\,RT\)
\(= \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\)

where \(\Delta n_g\) is the difference between the number of moles of gaseous products and those of gaseous reactants.

Note that for reactions involving only solids and liquids \(\Delta V\) is very small, so \(\Delta H = \Delta U\); and for a gas-phase reaction in which \(\Delta n_g = 0\), \(\Delta H\) is again equal to \(\Delta U\).

STATEMENT : Hess's law of constant heat summation states that overall the enthalpy change for a reaction is equal to the sum of enthalpy changes of individual steps in the reaction.

The enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is the same regardless of the path by which the reaction occurs. Hess's law is a direct consequence of the fact that enthalpy is a state function — the enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states and not on the path followed. To obtain the overall equation, the individual steps are added or subtracted like algebraic entities.

EXAMPLE : consider the synthesis of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\)
i. \(\mathrm{2H_2(g) + N_2(g) \longrightarrow N_2H_4(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H_1^0 = +95.4\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
ii. \(\mathrm{N_2H_4(g) + H_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,NH_3(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H_2^0 = -187.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Adding,
\(\mathrm{3\,H_2(g) + N_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,NH_3(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = 95.4 - 187.6 = -92.2\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The sum of the enthalpy changes for steps (i) and (ii) equals the enthalpy change for the overall reaction.

APPLICATIONS : Hess's law is useful to calculate the enthalpy changes of reactions whose enthalpies cannot be measured experimentally — for instance reactions that are too slow, that cannot be carried out in isolation, or whose products are contaminated by side reactions. It also allows standard enthalpies of formation, combustion, bond enthalpies and enthalpies of hypothetical reactions to be obtained indirectly from other measurable enthalpy changes.

\(\mathrm{2H_2(g) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2H_2O(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta S = -327\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\), \(\Delta H = -572\ \mathrm{kJ}\) at 298 K

The entropy of the SYSTEM does decrease, since three moles of gas become two moles of liquid. But the second law requires the TOTAL entropy of system plus surroundings to increase, not the entropy of the system alone.

The reaction is strongly exothermic, so 572 kJ of heat is released to the surroundings at constant pressure and 298 K. The entropy change of the surroundings is
\(\Delta S_{surr} = -\dfrac{\Delta H}{T} = \dfrac{572 \times 10^3\ \mathrm{J}}{298\ \mathrm{K}} = +1919\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)

Therefore
\(\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr}\)
\(= -327\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}} + 1919\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)
\(= +1592\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)

Since \(\Delta S_{total} > 0\), the reaction is spontaneous. The large positive entropy change of the surroundings, produced by the heat released, more than compensates for the decrease in the entropy of the system.

(The same conclusion follows from \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -572 - 298(-0.327) = -474.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\), which is negative.)

The total entropy change accompanying a process is
\(\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S + \Delta S_{surr}\)

If \(\Delta H\) is the enthalpy change of the system, the enthalpy change of the surroundings is \(-\Delta H\), so
\(\Delta S_{surr} = -\dfrac{\Delta H}{T}\)

Substituting,
\(\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S - \dfrac{\Delta H}{T}\)

Multiplying throughout by \(T\) and rearranging,
\(T\,\Delta S_{total} = T\,\Delta S - \Delta H\)
or \(\Delta H - T\Delta S = -T\,\Delta S_{total}\)

Since \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\),
\(\Delta G = -T\,\Delta S_{total}\)

COMMENT ON SPONTANEITY. Because \(T\) is always positive, \(\Delta G\) and \(\Delta S_{total}\) always have opposite signs:
i. \(\Delta S_{total} > 0\) and \(\Delta G < 0\) — the process is spontaneous;
ii. \(\Delta S_{total} < 0\) and \(\Delta G > 0\) — the process is nonspontaneous;
iii. \(\Delta S_{total} = 0\) and \(\Delta G = 0\) — the process is at equilibrium.

The advantage of the Gibbs energy criterion is that \(\Delta G\) is expressed in terms of the properties of the SYSTEM only, so the surroundings need not be examined separately.

\(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V = -P_{ext}\,(V_2 - V_1)\)

The gas is compressed, so work is done ON the system and \(W = +36.0\ \mathrm{J}\).
\(P_{ext} = 1.2 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\), \(V_1 = 500\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 500 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}\)

Substituting,
\(36.0\ \mathrm{J} = -1.2 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{Pa} \times (V_2 - 500 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3})\)

\(V_2 - 500 \times 10^{-6} = -\dfrac{36.0}{1.2 \times 10^5} = -3.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}\)

\(V_2 = 5.0 \times 10^{-4} - 3.0 \times 10^{-4} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}\)

The final volume is \(2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3} = 200\ \mathrm{cm^3}\), which is smaller than the initial 500 \(\mathrm{cm^3}\), as a compression requires.

The expansion is isothermal and reversible, so
\(W_{max} = -2.303\,nRT \log_{10} \dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\)

Molar mass of \(\mathrm{O_2} = 32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(n = \dfrac{24\ \mathrm{g}}{32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.75\ \mathrm{mol}\)
\(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\), \(P_1 = 1.6\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(P_2 = 1\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(W_{max} = -2.303 \times 0.75\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K} \times \log_{10} \dfrac{1.6}{1}\)
\(= -2.303 \times 0.75 \times 8.314 \times 298 \times 0.2041\)
\(= -873.5\ \mathrm{J}\)

The maximum work is \(-873.5\ \mathrm{J}\) (about \(-0.87\) kJ). The negative sign shows the work is done BY the gas on the surroundings, as expected for an expansion.

[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(\mathrm{Ans. : (-18.6\ kJ)}\). That is the answer for TWO moles of \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}\) — it is the value the book itself prints for Q.4 (xx), which asks about 2 moles of the same decomposition at the same temperature. This question specifies 132 g, and since \(M(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}) = 80\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) that is 1.65 mol, giving \(\Delta n_g = 4.95\) and \(W = -15.35\) kJ. The key is self-refuting: the same reaction at the same temperature cannot do identical work for 1.65 mol and for 2 mol.]

\(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3(s) \longrightarrow N_2O(g) + 2\,H_2O(g)}\)

Work done in a chemical reaction is
\(W = -\Delta n_g RT\)

Molar mass of \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3} = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(n = \dfrac{132\ \mathrm{g}}{80\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 1.65\ \mathrm{mol}\)

One mole of \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3(s)}\) gives \(1 + 2 = 3\) moles of gas and no gaseous reactant, so for 1.65 mol
\(\Delta n_g = 3 \times 1.65 = 4.95\ \mathrm{mol}\)
\(T = 100^\circ\mathrm{C} = 373\ \mathrm{K}\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(W = -4.95\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 373\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(= -15351\ \mathrm{J} = -15.35\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Since \(W\) is negative, work is done BY the system on the surroundings — as expected, because the decomposition of a solid produces gas and the system expands.

\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s) + 3CO(g) \longrightarrow 2\,Fe(s) + 3CO_2(g)}\)

\(\Delta_r H^0 = \sum \Delta_f H^0(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_f H^0(\text{reactants})\)
\(= [2\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{Fe}) + 3\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CO_2})] - [\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}) + 3\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CO})]\)

Fe(s) is an element in its standard state, so \(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{Fe}) = 0\).

\(= [2 \times 0 + 3 \times (-393)] - [(-824) + 3 \times (-110)]\)
\(= -1179 - (-824 - 330)\)
\(= -1179 + 1154\)
\(= -25\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The standard enthalpy of the reaction is \(-25\ \mathrm{kJ}\); the reaction is exothermic.

\(\Delta G = \Delta H^0 - T\Delta S^0\)
\(\Delta H^0 = 219\ \mathrm{kJ} = +219\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
\(\Delta S^0 = -21\ \mathrm{J/K} = -21 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ/K}\)

\(\Delta G = 219\ \mathrm{kJ} - T \times (-21 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}})\)
\(= 219\ \mathrm{kJ} + (21 \times 10^{-3})\,T\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Both terms are positive for every positive value of \(T\), so \(\Delta G > 0\) at all temperatures. At 298 K, for instance, \(\Delta G = 219 + 6.26 = +225.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

The reaction is therefore NONSPONTANEOUS, and it is nonspontaneous at every temperature — it is the case in which \(\Delta H\) is positive and \(\Delta S\) is negative, so no temperature can make \(\Delta G\) negative and there is no cross-over temperature.

\(\mathrm{2\,H_2O(\mathit{l}) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2H_2O_2(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta H^0 = 196\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(\Delta S^0 = -126\ \mathrm{J/K}\)

Under standard state conditions \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\).

\(\Delta G^0 = \Delta H^0 - T\Delta S^0\)
\(= 196\ \mathrm{kJ} - 298\ \mathrm{K} \times (-126 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}})\)
\(= 196\ \mathrm{kJ} + 37.5\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
\(= +233.5\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Since \(\Delta G^0\) is positive, the reaction is NONSPONTANEOUS under standard state conditions.

CROSS-OVER TEMPERATURE : a cross-over temperature exists only when \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) have the SAME sign, so that the two terms of \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) oppose each other. Here \(\Delta H^0\) is positive and \(\Delta S^0\) is negative, so \(-T\Delta S^0\) is positive too and
\(\Delta G = 196 + (126 \times 10^{-3})\,T\)
is positive at every temperature. NO, the reaction has no cross-over temperature; it is nonspontaneous at all temperatures.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_4(g) + HCl(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_5Cl(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -72.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(\Delta n_g\) = (moles of gaseous products) - (moles of gaseous reactants) \(= 1 - 2 = -1\ \mathrm{mol}\)

From \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\),
\(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT\)
\(= -72.3\ \mathrm{kJ} - (-1\ \mathrm{mol}) \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(= -72.3\ \mathrm{kJ} + 2.478\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
\(= -69.8\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The \(PV\) work is
\(W = -\Delta n_g RT = -(-1) \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3} \times 298 = +2.48\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

So \(\Delta U = -69.8\ \mathrm{kJ}\) and \(2.48\ \mathrm{kJ}\) of \(PV\) work is done. The positive sign shows the work is done ON the system, which is expected since two moles of gas contract to one and the system is compressed by the surroundings.

\(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V = -P_{ext}\,(V_2 - V_1)\)
\(P_{ext} = 43\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(V_1 = 8.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(V_2 = 4.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

\(W = -43\ \mathrm{bar} \times (4.0\ \mathrm{dm^3} - 8.0\ \mathrm{dm^3})\)
\(= -43 \times (-4.0) = +172\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar}\)

Using \(1\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} = 100\ \mathrm{J}\),
\(W = 172 \times 100 = 17200\ \mathrm{J} = +17.2\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The work done is \(+17.2\ \mathrm{kJ}\). The positive sign means work is done ON the system by the surroundings, so the work energy FLOWS INTO the system. This is consistent with the volume decreasing during the synthesis of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), in which four moles of gas \((\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2})\) become two moles of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(\mathrm{Ans. : (a = +983\ kJ\,;\ b = 0\ kJ)}\). The NUMBER for part (a) is correct but the UNIT is wrong by a factor of 1000 — oxidising one mole of HCl changes the gas count by only \(\Delta n_g = -0.25\ \mathrm{mol}\), so \(W = 0.25 \times 8.314 \times 473 = +983\) J, i.e. about \(+0.983\) kJ, not \(+983\) kJ. Part (b) is correct.]

Work done in a chemical reaction is \(W = -\Delta n_g RT\).

(a) \(\mathrm{4HCl(g) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,Cl_2(g) + 2\,H_2O(g)}\)
For the equation as written, \(\Delta n_g = (2 + 2) - (4 + 1) = -1\ \mathrm{mol}\) per 4 moles of HCl.
For the oxidation of ONE mole of HCl,
\(\Delta n_g = \dfrac{-1}{4} = -0.25\ \mathrm{mol}\)
\(T = 200^\circ\mathrm{C} = 473\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(W = -(-0.25\ \mathrm{mol}) \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 473\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(= +983\ \mathrm{J}\) (about \(+0.983\) kJ)

The positive sign shows work is done ON the system, since the number of moles of gas decreases.

(b) \(\mathrm{2\,NO(g) \longrightarrow N_2(g) + O_2(g)}\)
\(\Delta n_g = (1 + 1) - 2 = 0\)

\(W = -0 \times RT = 0\)

No \(PV\) work is done, because the number of moles of gaseous products equals the number of moles of gaseous reactants and the volume does not change. This is true for one mole of NO as well, since scaling a reaction with \(\Delta n_g = 0\) leaves \(\Delta n_g\) zero.

[Textbook misprint: the prose of the question names the reactant "CIF" (with a capital i). The printed equation shows it correctly as \(\mathrm{ClF}\), chlorine monofluoride. The answer is unaffected.]

\(\mathrm{2\,ClF(g) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow Cl_2O(g) + OF_2(g)}\)

The standard enthalpy of the reaction refers to the equation as written, that is, to ONE mole of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

Molar mass of \(\mathrm{O_2} = 32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(n = \dfrac{6.0\ \mathrm{g}}{32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.1875\ \mathrm{mol}\)

The enthalpy change accompanying the reaction of 0.1875 mol of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is 38.55 kJ, so for 1 mol of \(\mathrm{O_2}\)

\(\Delta_r H^0 = \dfrac{38.55\ \mathrm{kJ}}{0.1875\ \mathrm{mol}} \times 1\ \mathrm{mol} = 205.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The standard enthalpy of the reaction is \(+205.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\); the reaction is endothermic.

The required reaction is the formation of one mole of \(\mathrm{CH_3OH(\mathit{l})}\) from its elements in their standard states:
\(\mathrm{C(graphite) + 2H_2(g) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow CH_3OH(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta_f H^0 = ?\)

By Hess's law, reverse equation (i) and add equation (ii) once and equation (iii) twice.

Reversed (i) : \(\mathrm{CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(\mathit{l}) \longrightarrow CH_3OH(\mathit{l}) + \tfrac{3}{2}\,O_2(g)}\), \(\Delta H^0 = +726\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
(ii) : \(\mathrm{C(graphite) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow CO_2(g)}\), \(\Delta H^0 = -393\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
(iii) \(\times\) 2 : \(\mathrm{2H_2(g) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2H_2O(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta H^0 = 2 \times (-286) = -572\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Adding the three equations, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{2H_2O}\) cancel and \(\tfrac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{O_2}\) on the right cancels \(\tfrac{3}{2}\) of the \(2\,\mathrm{O_2}\) on the left, leaving
\(\mathrm{C(graphite) + 2H_2(g) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow CH_3OH(\mathit{l})}\)

\(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CH_3OH}) = +726 - 393 - 572 = -239\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The standard enthalpy of formation of liquid methanol is \(-239\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

[Textbook misprint: equation (iii) is printed as \(\mathrm{H_2B_4O_7(s) \longrightarrow 2P_2O_3(s) + H_2O(\mathit{l})}\). A boron compound cannot yield a phosphorus oxide; the species intended is \(\mathrm{2B_2O_3(s)}\), which is the compound equation (i) produces, balances the boron and oxygen exactly, and is the only reading under which the Hess cycle closes on the target reaction. The stem is transcribed as printed and solved on that reading.]

Target : \(\mathrm{H_2B_4O_7(s) + H_2O(\mathit{l}) \longrightarrow 4HBO_2(aq)}\)

By Hess's law, take (iii) as written, (i) reversed and doubled, and (ii) multiplied by 4.

(iii) : \(\mathrm{H_2B_4O_7(s) \longrightarrow 2B_2O_3(s) + H_2O(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta H^0 = +17.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
Reversed (i) \(\times\) 2 : \(\mathrm{2B_2O_3(s) + 6H_2O(\mathit{l}) \longrightarrow 4H_3BO_3(aq)}\), \(\Delta H^0 = -2 \times 14.4 = -28.8\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
(ii) \(\times\) 4 : \(\mathrm{4H_3BO_3(aq) \longrightarrow 4HBO_2(aq) + 4H_2O(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta H^0 = 4 \times (-0.02) = -0.08\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Adding, \(\mathrm{2B_2O_3}\) and \(\mathrm{4H_3BO_3}\) cancel, and of the water \(6\,\mathrm{H_2O}\) on the left is offset by \(1 + 4 = 5\,\mathrm{H_2O}\) on the right, leaving one \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) on the left:
\(\mathrm{H_2B_4O_7(s) + H_2O(\mathit{l}) \longrightarrow 4HBO_2(aq)}\)

\(\Delta H^0 = 17.3 - 28.8 - 0.08 = -11.58\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The standard enthalpy change of the reaction at 298 K is \(-11.58\ \mathrm{kJ}\); the reaction is exothermic.

Molar mass of water \(= 18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(n = \dfrac{180\ \mathrm{g}}{18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 10\ \mathrm{mol}\)

(a) MELTING the ice at \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\)
\(Q_a = n \times \Delta_{fus}H^0 = 10\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.01\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} = 60.1\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

(b) HEATING the water from \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\)
\(Q_b = m \times c \times \Delta T = 180\ \mathrm{g} \times 4.18\ \mathrm{J\ g^{-1}\ K^{-1}} \times 100\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(= 75240\ \mathrm{J} = 75.24\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

(c) VAPOURISING the water at \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\)
\(Q_c = n \times \Delta_{vap}H^0 = 10\ \mathrm{mol} \times 40.7\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} = 407\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

TOTAL heat required
\(Q = Q_a + Q_b + Q_c = 60.1 + 75.24 + 407 = 542.34\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Hence about \(542.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\) of heat is required. All three steps absorb heat, so the total is positive.

[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(W = +10.13\) J and \(\Delta U = -609.9\) J. Those values follow from the litre-atmosphere conversion \(1\ \mathrm{L\ atm} = 101.325\ \mathrm{J}\), but the stem states the pressure as 1 BAR, and this chapter's own §4.4.2 gives \(1\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} = 100\ \mathrm{J}\) and uses it throughout Problems 4.1, 4.3 and 4.6. At 1 bar the work is exactly \(+10.0\) J and \(\Delta U = -610\) J. The difference is small (1.3%) but the book contradicts its own stated conversion.]

\(\mathrm{C_2H_4(g) + H_2(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_6(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -620\ \mathrm{J}\)

The gases react at 1 bar, and 100 mL of each reactant gives 100 mL of product (one mole of \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\) reacts with one mole of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) to give one mole of \(\mathrm{C_2H_6}\)).
\(V_1 = 100\ \mathrm{mL} + 100\ \mathrm{mL} = 200\ \mathrm{mL} = 0.2\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)
\(V_2 = 100\ \mathrm{mL} = 0.1\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

PRESSURE-VOLUME WORK
\(W = -P_{ext}\,(V_2 - V_1) = -1\ \mathrm{bar} \times (0.1 - 0.2)\ \mathrm{dm^3} = +0.1\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar}\)

Using the conversion given in this chapter, \(1\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} = 100\ \mathrm{J}\),
\(W = +0.1 \times 100 = +10.0\ \mathrm{J}\)

The positive sign shows work is done ON the system, as expected since two volumes of gas contract to one.

CHANGE IN INTERNAL ENERGY
\(\Delta U = Q + W\), and at constant pressure \(Q_p = \Delta H\), so
\(\Delta U = \Delta H + W = -620\ \mathrm{J} + 10.0\ \mathrm{J} = -610\ \mathrm{J}\)

Hence \(W = +10.0\ \mathrm{J}\) and \(\Delta U = -610\ \mathrm{J}\).

\(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3(s) \longrightarrow N_2O(g) + 2H_2O(g)}\)

\(W = -\Delta n_g RT\)

One mole of \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3(s)}\) produces \(1 + 2 = 3\) moles of gas and there is no gaseous reactant, so for 2 moles of \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}\)
\(\Delta n_g = 2 \times 3 = 6\ \mathrm{mol}\)
\(T = 100^\circ\mathrm{C} = 373\ \mathrm{K}\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(W = -6\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 373\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(= -18607\ \mathrm{J} = -18.61\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Since \(W\) is negative, WORK IS DONE BY THE SYSTEM on the surroundings. The solid decomposes into six moles of gas, so the system expands against the external pressure and loses energy as work.
